opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's useful to be honest about where AlphaFold actually sits in the overall process. AlphaFold was a phenomenal breakthrough. It took a problem people had worked on for fifty years, predicting the 3D structure of a protein from its sequence, and essentially cracked it. But structure prediction is one piece of a very long chain of problems you have to solve to go from "here's a disease" to "here's a molecule that safely treats it in a patient."

If you lay that chain out, you start to see how many other AlphaFold-sized problems are sitting there. Knowing a protein's structure isn't the same as knowing how a small molecule will bind to it, how tightly, and with what kinetics. Then you need to know whether that molecule binds anything else in the body, because off-target effects are where a lot of toxicity comes from. You need to understand whether it can be made, whether it's soluble, whether it gets absorbed, where it distributes, how it's metabolized, how long it sticks around. Beyond that you're asking whether hitting this target actually changes the disease, which is really a question about biology at the level of cells, tissues and whole organisms. Each of those is a hard scientific problem in its own right, and today most of them are still answered largely by experiment, iteration and a lot of expensive trial and error.

So when I say roughly half a dozen, I'm not claiming a precise number. It's more a way of saying: look at the major failure points in drug discovery, the reasons molecules die in the lab or in the clinic, and ask which of those we can currently model with real predictive accuracy. Right now, very few. Each one that we turn into something you can reliably compute, rather than having to discover empirically, is a step change comparable to what AlphaFold did for structure.

The exciting part is that these breakthroughs compound. AlphaFold-style models give you better inputs for binding prediction; better binding prediction makes selectivity modeling more tractable; and so on. And the goal, at least the one we're working toward, is that eventually you're doing most of the design in silico, with the lab used to confirm rather than to search. We're not there yet. But it's no longer science fiction, it's a roadmap, and you can see the pieces that need to fall into place.

r001.rationale: The response says other drug-discovery problems need reliable predictive models and are currently addressed empirically, but it does not clearly specify that those models must reach experimental-level accuracy.

r002.rationale: It explains that knowing structure or predicting binding is not enough: a suitable drug must also avoid off-target effects, have workable properties, and affect the disease.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing people get wrong about AlphaFold is they treat it as if it solved biology, and really it solved one very specific, very well-posed problem: given this sequence, what does the static structure look like? And that was an incredible result, don't get me wrong. But if you actually walk through what it takes to go from "here's a disease" to "here's a pill in a patient," structure prediction is maybe one step out of a long chain, and most of the other steps are, honestly, in a worse state than protein folding was in 2016.

So let me just enumerate a few. The first is binding. Knowing the structure of a protein tells you very little about which small molecules will actually bind to it, how tightly, and how that changes when the protein moves, because proteins aren't static, they're flopping around constantly. Getting a model that predicts binding affinity to the accuracy a medicinal chemist actually needs, where the difference between a good drug and a useless one is a factor of ten in potency, that's an AlphaFold-sized problem on its own. We're making progress on it, but we're not there.

Then there's the problem of dynamics and conformational change. A lot of the interesting targets, things like GPCRs or ion channels or disordered regions, don't have a single structure. They have ensembles. And a huge fraction of what makes them druggable or undruggable lives in that ensemble behavior. We don't have a great generative model of how proteins move yet.

Then you go up a level, and you're not dealing with one protein anymore, you're dealing with the cell. You can have a molecule that binds perfectly to your target in a test tube and does nothing useful in a cell, because of transport, because of off-target effects, because the pathway compensates. Predicting what happens when you perturb a cell is a fundamentally different problem from predicting a structure. It's much more like a systems problem, and the data is messier and more expensive to get.

Then there's the whole ADMET side, so absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, toxicity. Is this thing orally bioavailable? Does the liver chew it up in twenty minutes? Is it going to cause cardiac issues at the dose you need? Those are the things that kill most drugs in the clinic, and they're currently handled with a mix of heuristics and expensive animal studies. A model that could reliably predict those properties would be transformative on its own.

And then the last one, which is maybe the hardest, is the question of what to target in the first place. Which protein, which mechanism, actually matters for this disease in actual humans? That's a biology question, and the honest answer is that most of our hypotheses are wrong. Clinical trials fail mostly for efficacy reasons, not safety reasons, which means we picked the wrong target or the wrong hypothesis. Fixing that requires understanding disease biology at a level we really don't have.

So when I say half a dozen breakthroughs, I'm being a bit loose with the number, but each of those is a problem that looks, to me, roughly as hard and roughly as important as structure prediction did a decade ago. And I think the exciting thing is that the recipe that worked for AlphaFold, which is large models, the right inductive biases, and crucially the right data at scale, is probably applicable to several of them. But the data piece is the hard part. For structure we had the PDB, decades of carefully curated experiments. For most of these other problems the equivalent dataset doesn't exist yet, so part of the work is actually going out and generating it, which is why I think the labs that can do both the wet lab and the ML side together have a real advantage here.

r001.rationale: The response identifies several difficult drug-design problems and says binding predictions need medicinal-chemist-level accuracy, but it does not characterize the breakthroughs generally as achieving experimental-level accuracy across other fundamental biology and chemistry concepts.

r002.rationale: It explains that a molecule can bind its target perfectly in a test tube yet do nothing useful in a cell because of transport, off-target effects, or pathway compensation.

astra-6.text:
Because predicting a protein’s structure is one incredibly important piece of the puzzle, but it’s still a long way from designing a drug that works in a patient. You need to understand which biological mechanism to intervene in, how to design a molecule that changes that mechanism, and whether that molecule can reach the right tissue, have the intended effect, and do so safely.

Those are connected problems, but solving one doesn’t automatically solve the others. Even knowing a protein’s structure doesn’t tell you everything about how it moves, how it interacts with other molecules, or what happens when you perturb it in a living system.

So I wouldn’t take half a dozen as a precise count. The point is that we need breakthroughs of comparable significance across several layers of biology and chemistry. And we need to connect those models to experiments, so that we can test their predictions and learn from where they’re wrong. That’s what would move us from predicting something about biology to reliably designing an intervention that changes it.

r001.rationale: It calls for major breakthroughs across biology and chemistry and says models should connect to experiments, but does not clearly state that those breakthroughs must achieve experimental-level accuracy for other fundamental concepts.

r002.rationale: It explains that changing the biological mechanism is only one part of drug design; the molecule must also reach the right tissue, produce the intended effect, and do so safely.

sol-6.1.text:
AlphaFold solved a really important piece of the puzzle: given a protein’s sequence, what does its structure look like? But designing a drug means solving a whole chain of problems beyond that. What should you target to change the course of a disease? How do you design a molecule that interacts with that target in exactly the right way? And how do you make sure it reaches the right place in the body, has the effect you want, and doesn’t cause toxicity?

Those are distinct scientific challenges, and being very good at one doesn’t automatically solve the others. Even knowing a protein’s structure doesn’t tell you everything about how it moves, how it interacts with other molecules, or what happens when you intervene in a living system.

So I wouldn’t take the number six too literally. The point is that we need several breakthroughs of comparable significance, connected together. That’s what could take us from a remarkable ability to predict one aspect of biology to an ability to reliably design medicines.

r001.rationale: The response calls for several breakthroughs of comparable significance and lists drug-design challenges, but does not characterize them as achieving experimental-level accuracy for other fundamental concepts in biology and chemistry.

r002.rationale: The response explains that drug suitability also depends on reaching the right place in the body, producing the desired effect, and avoiding toxicity; target interaction alone is not enough.
